title: Mary Anderson's windscreen wiper
hook: A tram ride in New York sleet led one woman to invent the windscreen wiper.
peek: On a winter visit to New York, Mary Anderson saw a tram driver struggling to see through his snowy front window. She went home to Alabama and designed a hand-operated wiper, patented in 1903.
lede: During a trip to New York City around the winter of 1902, Mary Anderson of Birmingham, Alabama, rode a streetcar through sleet. The story goes that the driver had to open the front window and lean out to clear the glass, letting the cold in on everyone. Anderson sketched a fix, and in November 1903 she received a US patent for a window cleaning device.

bullets.text: Her wiper was a swinging arm with a rubber blade, worked by a lever inside the vehicle. The driver could clear the glass without stopping, and the arm could be taken off in fine weather.
Anderson offered the rights to manufacturers, including a firm in Canada. They told her the device had too little commercial value to be worth making.

bullets.opening: A patent that ran out early
bullets.text: Her patent lasted 17 years and expired in 1920, just as car ownership was booming. Wipers soon became standard on cars, but Anderson never earned money from the idea.
Anderson's work was largely forgotten for decades. In 2011 she was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for the windscreen wiper.
